article.Citation/Title: Terasaki, D., Loh, R., Cornell, A., Taub, J., & Thurstone, C. (2022). Single-dose intravenous ketamine or intramuscular naltrexone for high-utilization inpatients with alcohol use disorder: pilot trial feasibility and readmission rates. Addiction Science & Clinical Practice, 17, 64.
article.InterventionDescription: IV ketamine 0.5 mg/kg over 40 min or IM naltrexone 380 mg single dose, bedside pre-discharge; open-label; brief pre-infusion counseling; safety-net hospital inpatient setting.

article.Outcome: Methods/Outcomes and the Abstract both explicitly designate 'the primary clinical outcome was 30-day, all-cause hospital readmission rate.' Of the two pairwise comparisons reported against the linkage-alone (LA) control (Results/'Primary clinical outcome'; Table 2), this record uses the ketamine (KET) vs LA comparison — RR = 0.37 (p = 0.17) — rather than the naltrexone (NTX) vs LA comparison (RR = 0.52), because naltrexone is not a psychedelic and sets no substance flag in this database; ketamine is the article's only psychedelic intervention, and the substance flags on this record (Ketamine=1 only) are scoped to it. Note: 30-day readmission is a healthcare-utilization outcome, not itself a classic SUD-behavior measure. The article's substance-use-specific data — baseline/follow-up TLFB drinking quantity and the post-hoc 'alcohol-related readmission' subclassification (Results, 'When analyzing alcohol-related readmissions post-hoc...') — are secondary/exploratory and underpowered (TLFB follow-up obtained from only 6/13 KET participants). Per the prompt's boundary-case rule ('trials whose only SUD outcome is secondary are eligible... Outcome is still the stated primary outcome's effect size'), EligibleYN=Y rests on these secondary SUD elements while Outcome is coded to the stated primary (readmission) effect size.
article.SD: No confidence interval, standard error, or chi-squared value is printed alongside the KET-vs-LA RR of 0.37; Table 2 and the Results text give only the RR point estimate and 'p=0.17'. The Statistical analysis section states relative risks were derived from chi-squared tests of independence, but no chi^2 statistic is printed for this specific 2-arm comparison. Coded '.' rather than back-computing an unreported statistic.
article.PVal: Results/'Primary clinical outcome': 'Comparing the KET arm to the LA arm, the relative risk of readmission was 0.37 (p = 0.17)'; matches Table 2 ('RR to LA arm 0.3736' / 'p=0.17').
article.SampleSize_NFinal: Table 2 column headers give KET n=13 and LA n=17 for the readmission comparison (13+17=30). All 44 randomized participants had readmission ascertainable via EHR query with no loss to follow-up for this outcome (Methods/Statistical analysis: primary and secondary clinical outcomes 'did not require participant responses, so all participants were included in intent-to-treat analysis'), but the specific KET-vs-LA effect size excludes the 14 NTX-arm participants, giving a denominator of 30, not 44.

MethodologyDescribedYN.note: All elements described except a priori sample-size/power justification: N=44 reflects a one-year pragmatic pilot enrollment window, not a calculated target, and the only power-adjacent statement is a post hoc admission in Limitations that the study 'was under-powered for detecting statistically significant differences.' Blinding is met as 'described' because the article states explicitly there was no blinding ('open-label'; 'There was no blinding in this study'), which satisfies the described-vs-present distinction even though BlindingYN=0.

article.Pos Result Y/N: Coded 0 (null), not 1. The ketamine arm trended favorably on the primary outcome (15.4% vs 41.2% readmission, RR=0.37) but this was explicitly nonsignificant (p=0.17), and the article itself frames the result as promising but inconclusive ('differences were non-significant'; Conclusions: 'showed promise ... though differences were non-significant'). Per USPSTF-strict interpretation, a favorable but nonsignificant primary-outcome trend is coded as a null result, not a positive one.
article.Comparator: Comparator=1. The primary comparator is the linkage-alone (LA) arm (n=17): standard enhanced-linkage-to-care with no pharmacologic intervention. A second active-drug arm (IM naltrexone, not a psychedelic) was also run in parallel but is not itself the comparator used for this record's Outcome (see Outcome rationale).
article.RecruitmentRepresentYN: Coded 1: participants were drawn from the actual consecutive census of the hospital's addiction consultation service (real inpatient clinical population), not recruited via advertisement/volunteer solicitation, and the authors describe the design as 'very pragmatic' (Strengths). Flagged as non-obvious because screening was still substantial — of 205 assessed, 96 (47%) met exclusion criteria, mostly medical comorbidities specific to ketamine/naltrexone safety (cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, opioid use) — so the enrolled sample, while drawn from a real clinical population, was meaningfully narrowed by drug-safety exclusions.
article.Retention (%): Coded 50 = 22/44 (14-day addiction-clinic attendance across all arms: KET 8/13, NTX 7/14, LA 7/17; Table 2). This study reports several different 'completion' metrics with different denominators: the primary readmission outcome was ascertained for all 44/44 (100%) via EHR regardless of patient contact, while only 18/44 (40.9%) provided re-assessment data (PHQ9/TLFB/acceptability) at follow-up. 14-day clinic attendance is used here as the best single 'retention' figure because it is the study's own explicitly reported follow-up engagement metric applied uniformly across arms; the alternative denominators are noted here rather than silently discarded.
article.RaceEthnicity_BIPOCPercent: Table 1, All Arms (n=44) race breakdown: White/Caucasian 25 (56.8%), Black/African American 3 (6.8%), American Indian/Alaska Native 7 (15.9%), Multiple/Other 9 (20.5%). Non-white sum = 3+7+9 = 19/44 = 43.2%. Hispanic/Latinx ethnicity (15/44, 34.1%) is reported as a separate crosscutting category per the article's own table structure and is not added to the race-based BIPOC figure, consistent with the field rule that ethnicity crosses racial categories.
article.Country_USvsNonUS: Single US site: 'urban, academic, safety-net hospital' — Denver Health & Hospital Association, Denver, Colorado, USA (Author details).
article.SocioeconomicStatusYN: Coded 1: eligibility required 'public (e.g., Medicaid) or private insurance,' the site is explicitly a 'safety-net' hospital, and Table 1 reports housing status including 'not stably housed / unknown' for 38.6% of the sample — an explicit low-SES-relevant description.
article.ConfoundYN: Coded 1: Discussion explicitly identifies and discusses baseline imbalances across arms as possible confounders despite randomization ('the linkage alone arm appeared to be more male, have higher baseline hospital utilization, and be less stably housed... these factors may have biased in favor of pharmacologic intervention'), and reports a post-hoc per-protocol sensitivity analysis adjusting for protocol deviations.
article.InterventionTherapy: Coded 1: the KET arm received brief structured pre-infusion counseling (advice to focus on deep breathing and approach difficult experiences with curiosity, plus a standardized relaxation soundtrack) — preparatory support beyond bare drug administration. All arms also received 'enhanced linkage' to outpatient addiction care, which is a care-coordination component rather than psychotherapy itself; the pre-infusion counseling is the basis for coding 1.
article.ReductionMeasured: Coded 1: self-reported daily drinking quantity/frequency was captured at baseline via a modified Timeline Follow Back and re-assessed at the follow-up clinic visit (Methods/Outcomes; Results: 'Some data elements were re-assessed at the addiction clinic follow-up visit (including PHQ9, TLFB...)'), functioning as a partial-reduction-type drinking measure even though the low follow-up rate precluded robust analysis.
article.CessationMeasured: Coded 0: no abstinence/complete-cessation rate is reported as a distinct outcome; TLFB tracked drinking quantity/frequency (reduction-type), not an abstinence endpoint.
article.RelapseMeasured: Coded 0: the study does not track relapse/return-to-drinking as its own outcome. Hospital readmission and ED visits are healthcare-utilization proxies, not an explicit relapse-to-use measure, and are coded as the primary/secondary clinical outcomes instead.
article.Followup in months: Longest reported outcome horizon is the 30-day all-cause readmission window (Methods/Outcomes), measured from hospital discharge (end of the single-dose intervention) = 1 month. No longer horizon is reported for this study's own data (the 3-month naltrexone retention figure cited in Discussion belongs to a different study, Busch et al.).
article.ArmScope: Coded 'psychedelic_arm.' Tables 5 and 6 report AE counts separately by arm (KET/NTX/LA); because naltrexone is not a psychedelic and this database's substance flags are scoped to the psychedelic intervention only (Ketamine=1), all ae_events and AE summary fields report KET-arm-only values, excluding NTX- and LA-only rows (e.g., an NTX-only injection-administration error with 'no ill effect' is not included in ae_events under this scope).
article.AE_denominator: Coded 13 = the full randomized/exposed KET arm, the broadest ketamine safety population. Sub-tables use smaller denominators for specific timepoints (Table 5 immediate symptom inquiry: n=12 of 13, one participant did not receive the intervention; Table 6 since-discharge PRISE: n=6 of 13, reflecting low follow-up attendance) — these are recorded in each ae_event's Description rather than collapsed into a single misleading denominator.
article.NParticipantsWithAE: Coded '.': the article reports per-symptom counts at two different, partially overlapping KET sub-samples (n=12 immediate, n=6 follow-up) without a deduplicated count of unique KET participants experiencing at least one AE across both assessments, so this cannot be computed without fabricating a number.

ae_events.Terasaki 2022_AE09: Results/'Acceptability and safety': CADSS mean 20.31 (SD 16.62) in the KET arm (n=12), described as 'nearly identical to that seen in a similar trial.' Per rubric core adaptation principle, in-session dissociative/CEQ-type phenomenology is expected with ketamine and is graded by consequence, not intensity; no intervention or persistence beyond the session is reported, so graded Mild with sufficient information (not indeterminate).
ae_events.Terasaki 2022_AE10: Results/'Acceptability and safety' and Table 4: KET arm mean SBP +12.66 mmHg (p=0.006) and DBP +10.34 mmHg (p=0.05) at 40 min, both attenuated at 160 min; article states 'no instances of treatment-emergent symptoms attributed to these vital sign changes.' Graded Mild with sufficient detail (explicit values, timepoints, resolution, no attributed symptoms or intervention) — not indeterminate.
ae_events.Terasaki 2022_AE11: Table 6 (adverse events since discharge reported at follow-up visit, KET n=6 of 13 randomized who provided follow-up data): diarrhea — 1/6 tolerable and 1/6 distressing. PRISE self-report gives only a tolerable/distressing rating, no CTCAE grade, intervention, or precise timing since discharge, so graded Mild by rubric default and flagged indeterminate. Onset banded 'delayed' because this was assessed at the outpatient follow-up visit after hospital discharge; the exact interval is not reported precisely (clinic intake was 'targeted within 7 days post-discharge' but attendance was often later or did not occur for most of the arm).

config_proposal.note: RR = 0.37 for 30-day all-cause readmission, ketamine arm vs linkage-alone arm (2/13 vs 7/17, Table 2), the article's stated primary clinical outcome. Direction flipped to -1 because RR<1 favors ketamine (fewer readmissions is the desired direction) — the raw RR scale is opposite the 'higher = more favorable' convention used for d/g. Confidence is 'approx' rather than 'clean': the comparison is nonsignificant (p=0.17) in a 13-vs-17 pilot subset of a 3-arm unblinded trial, excludes the parallel naltrexone arm entirely, and Discussion itself flags likely baseline imbalance biasing in favor of the drug arms — a methodologist would want to see these caveats before treating the RR as a clean point estimate.
